title: Class 2 Maths Syllabus: A Parent's Strand-by-Strand Guide + Free Quiz
meta_title: Class 2 Maths Syllabus: Parent Guide + Quiz
meta_desc: The full class 2 maths syllabus explained strand by strand: what mastery looks like, warning signs to watch, and a free 8-question quiz. Start today.
excerpt: Numbers to 999, regrouping, early multiplication, fractions, shapes, time and money — here is the whole Class 2 maths year in plain language, with the one warning sign to watch in each strand and a quick quiz to test your child.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
By the end of Class 1 a child can usually count to 100 and add small numbers. Then Class 2 arrives and the ground shifts fast: three-digit numbers, carrying and borrowing, the first taste of multiplication, and a clock they are suddenly expected to read. Parents in Tier 2 cities message me every June asking the same thing — what exactly is my child meant to learn this year? So here is the whole class 2 maths syllabus, strand by strand, in the order NCERT and most CBSE schools follow. For each one I have added what ‘mastery’ actually looks like and the single warning sign I would watch for. I am deliberately keeping each strand short; the aim is the map, not the turn-by-turn directions.

Numbers and place value up to 999

This is the backbone of the class 2 maths syllabus and everything else leans on it. A child should read, write and compare numbers up to 999, count in 2s, 5s and 10s, and — the part that matters most — understand that 3 in 347 means three hundreds, not just the digit three. Mastery looks like a child telling you that 347 is 300 + 40 + 7 without hesitating.

Warning sign: your child writes ‘two hundred and five’ as 2005. That is a place-value gap, not carelessness, and it is worth fixing before the addition unit.

Addition and subtraction with regrouping

Two- and three-digit sums, with carrying (regrouping) in addition and borrowing in subtraction. This is where a shaky place-value foundation shows up as tears. Mastery is solving 46 + 38 and 72 − 47 on paper correctly and, ideally, checking the answer by estimating first.

Warning sign: the child always writes the smaller digit taken from the larger regardless of position — so 72 − 47 becomes 35. It means they are treating each column separately instead of borrowing.

Introduction to multiplication and division

Class 2 does not demand full times-tables. It introduces multiplication as repeated addition (4 groups of 3 is 3 + 3 + 3 + 3) and division as equal sharing. The 2, 5 and 10 tables usually appear here. Mastery looks like a child drawing 3 rows of 4 dots and telling you it is both 3 × 4 and 4 + 4 + 4.

Warning sign: the child can chant ‘two fours are eight’ but cannot show you what it means with objects. Rote without meaning collapses in Class 3.

Fractions: half and quarter

Only the simplest fractions — one half and one quarter — as parts of a whole and of a small group. A roti cut in two, four children sharing four laddoos. Mastery is a child folding a paper square into two equal halves and knowing the halves must be the same size.

Warning sign: they call any two pieces ‘halves’ even when one is clearly bigger. The idea of equal parts is the whole point.

Shapes, space and symmetry

Here the strand covers 2D shapes (circle, triangle, square, rectangle), 3D solids (cube, cuboid, sphere, cone, cylinder), edges and corners, position words like near, far, above, below, and simple line symmetry. Mastery looks like a child sorting a ball, a dice and a matchbox into sphere, cube and cuboid and pointing out the fold line on a butterfly.

Warning sign: confusing a square with a cube, or a circle with a sphere — flat versus solid. Gently naming real objects fixes it fast.

Measurement: length, weight, capacity and time

A busy strand. Length in centimetres and metres, weight in grams and kilograms, capacity in litres, and telling time to the hour and half hour on a clock face, plus days of the week and months. Mastery is a child estimating that a pencil is about 12 cm and reading ‘half past 7’ on an analogue clock.

Warning sign: the child can only read a clock as digits and freezes at an analogue face. The moving hands are the skill the syllabus wants.

Money and data handling

Money means recognising rupee and paise coins and notes, making small amounts, and simple shopping sums — if a pencil costs ₹5 and an eraser ₹3, the total is ₹8. Data handling means reading a simple picture graph or tally chart. Mastery looks like a child counting out ₹15 in coins two different ways and telling you which fruit in a pictograph is the most popular.

Warning sign: the child adds the number of coins instead of their values — three ₹2 coins counted as ‘three rupees’. Value, not count, is the lesson.

The syllabus at a glance

Numbers to 999Reads 347 as 300 + 40 + 7Writes ‘two hundred five’ as 2005

Multiplication / divisionShows 3 × 4 as 3 rows of 4Chants tables with no meaning
FractionsFolds equal halvesCalls unequal pieces ‘halves’
Shapes & symmetrySorts cube, sphere, cuboidMixes flat with solid

Money & dataMakes ₹15 two waysCounts coins, not their value

How to use this map at home

You do not need to teach these in strict order, but I would keep them in roughly the sequence above, because each one quietly feeds the next. A few habits that help across every strand:

  • Anchor every new idea to a real object first — coins, a ruler, a folded roti — before touching a worksheet.
  • Ten focused minutes a day beats a long Sunday session; young attention spans are short and honest.
  • Rotate strands so the week mixes number work with shapes, time and money — variety keeps it from feeling like a grind.
  • When a warning sign shows up, slow down on that one strand rather than pushing ahead. The gap does not close by itself.

One honest caveat: schools vary in the order they teach these, and some ICSE syllabi push a little further on multiplication. If your school’s sequence differs, follow the school — this guide is the destination, not a fixed route.

Test where your child stands

The free quiz below samples across all these strands at Class 2 level — place value, regrouping, early multiplication, fractions, shapes, time and money. Let your child try it and read the explanations together for anything they miss; the misses tell you which strand to revisit. When you want structured written practice covering the whole year, the printable Class 2 workbook at the end has graded worksheets for every strand with answer keys, ready to print as often as you like.

quiz.title: Class 2 Maths Syllabus Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions sampling the whole Class 2 syllabus — place value, regrouping, multiplication, fractions, shapes, time and money. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: In the number 528, what does the digit 5 stand for?
questions.explanation: In 528 the 5 is in the hundreds place, so it stands for 5 hundreds, or 500.
6 + 8 = 14, so write 4 and carry 1. Then 4 + 3 + 1 = 8. The answer is 84.
You cannot take 7 from 2, so borrow: 12 − 7 = 5, then 6 − 4 = 2. The answer is 25.

questions.q: 3 groups of 4 apples is the same as which sum?
questions.explanation: 3 groups of 4 means 4 + 4 + 4 = 12, which is also 3 × 4.

questions.q: A roti is cut into two equal pieces. Each piece is called a
questions.explanation: Two equal parts of a whole are called halves, so each piece is one half.

questions.q: Which of these is a 3D solid, not a flat shape?
questions.explanation: A cube is a solid you can hold. A circle, triangle and square are flat 2D shapes.

questions.q: A clock shows the hour hand between 7 and 8 and the minute hand on 6. What is the time?
questions.explanation: The minute hand on 6 means half past, and the hour hand just past 7 means it is half past 7.

questions.q: You have three ₹2 coins. How much money is that in total?
questions.explanation: Add the values, not the number of coins: 2 + 2 + 2 = ₹6.

faq.q: What are the main topics in the Class 2 maths syllabus?
faq.a: Numbers and place value up to 999, addition and subtraction with regrouping, early multiplication and division, half and quarter fractions, 2D and 3D shapes with symmetry, measurement of length, weight, capacity and time, plus money and simple data handling.

faq.q: Is Class 2 maths harder than Class 1?
faq.a: It is a real step up. Numbers grow to three digits, carrying and borrowing arrive, and multiplication and clock-reading are brand new. A child who is fluent with place value handles the jump far more comfortably.
No. The syllabus introduces multiplication as repeated addition and usually covers only the 2, 5 and 10 tables. Understanding what 3 × 4 means matters more this year than memorising every table.

faq.q: How much daily maths practice is right for a Class 2 child?
faq.a: About ten to fifteen focused minutes a day, rotating strands through the week, works better than one long weekly session. Consistency and variety beat marathon study at this age.
